Sri Pada pilgrimage season 2026–2027: a journey to the sacred summit of Sri Lanka

Every year, as December approaches, thousands of pilgrims begin preparing for one of Sri Lanka’s most remarkable spiritual journeys. Their destination is Sri Pada, also known as Adam’s Peak, a majestic mountain in the island’s central highlands.

The 2026–2027 pilgrimage season is scheduled to begin on 23 December 2026, coinciding with Unduvap Full Moon Poya Day. It will continue until Vesak Full Moon Poya Day in 2027.

For some, the journey is an act of religious devotion. For others, it is a personal challenge, an opportunity to experience Sri Lanka’s mountain landscapes, or simply a chance to witness the unforgettable sight of sunrise from one of the island’s most sacred places.

Whatever brings them there, the climb to Sri Pada is an experience that stays with many visitors long after they return home.

A mountain sacred to many faiths

Rising to 2,243 metres above sea level, Sri Pada is one of the most recognisable mountains in Sri Lanka. Its distinctive conical summit can be seen from the surrounding highlands, but its importance goes far beyond its impressive appearance.

Near the top lies a sacred footprint-shaped impression in the rock. Different religious traditions associate it with different spiritual figures. Buddhists revere it as the footprint of the Buddha, Hindus associate it with Lord Shiva, while Muslim tradition connects it with Adam. Some Christian traditions associate the footprint with St Thomas.

This shared religious significance makes Sri Pada an extraordinary place. For centuries, people from different communities have made the journey to its summit, united by their own beliefs and traditions.

In Sri Lanka, the mountain is also closely associated with Saman, the guardian deity of the peak, who holds an important place in local Buddhist tradition.

The 2026–2027 pilgrimage season begins on 23 December

The new pilgrimage season will officially open on 23 December 2026, on Unduvap Full Moon Poya Day.

Preparations for the season have been discussed by local authorities and religious representatives, with arrangements focusing on the safety and convenience of the thousands of devotees expected to visit.

The opening is accompanied by traditional religious ceremonies and processions involving the sacred relic casket and the statue of God Saman. These ceremonial events are an important part of the annual tradition and mark the beginning of another pilgrimage season.

The season is expected to continue until Vesak Full Moon Poya Day in May 2027.

For travellers planning to visit, this is the period when the mountain becomes especially lively, with illuminated paths, roadside tea stalls and streams of pilgrims making their way towards the summit.

The night climb: a journey towards sunrise

One of the most distinctive aspects of the Sri Pada pilgrimage is that many people begin their ascent during the night.

Rather than climbing in the heat of the day, pilgrims usually set off after dark, following the illuminated staircase towards the summit. The route is made up of thousands of steps, with the main approach from Nallathanniya, also known as Dalhousie, being the most popular among visitors.

The ascent can take approximately three to four hours, depending on fitness, walking pace, weather conditions and the number of people on the trail.

Along the way, small shops and tea stalls offer refreshments and places to take a short break. During busy periods, the path can become crowded, particularly closer to the summit.

For many climbers, reaching the top before dawn is the highlight of the experience.

As the darkness gradually gives way to the first light of morning, the surrounding mountain ranges emerge from the shadows. On clear mornings, visitors may witness the famous triangular shadow of the peak stretching across the landscape.

It is a remarkable sight, and one of the reasons why so many people choose to make the climb during the night.

Choosing a route to the summit

There are several traditional routes leading to Sri Pada, including approaches from Nallathanniya, Ratnapura and Kuruwita.

The Nallathanniya route, on the Hatton side of the mountain, is the most frequently used by pilgrims and tourists. It is known for its long staircase and facilities along the way.

Other routes offer a different experience, passing through more remote forest landscapes. These journeys can be longer and require additional preparation.

Whichever route visitors choose, the climb should not be underestimated. The steep ascent, changing temperatures and physical demands make it important to be reasonably fit and prepared.

Comfortable walking shoes, warm clothing, drinking water and enough time for rest are essential. Visitors should also check local conditions before setting out.

A pilgrimage beyond the physical challenge

Although the climb attracts hikers and adventure seekers, Sri Pada is first and foremost a place of religious devotion.

During the pilgrimage season, visitors encounter people of all ages making their way towards the summit. Some climb with family members, others with groups of friends, while many undertake the journey as part of a long-standing religious tradition.

The atmosphere along the route is unlike that of an ordinary mountain hike. There are moments of quiet reflection, prayers, conversations and encouragement between strangers.

For many Sri Lankan devotees, reaching the summit is a deeply personal achievement. The journey is not simply about reaching the highest point, but about faith, perseverance and the experience of making the pilgrimage.

Visitors who are not taking part for religious reasons are welcome to appreciate the mountain’s cultural significance and should approach the experience with respect.

Visiting Sri Pada responsibly

Sri Pada is located within a sensitive natural environment, surrounded by forests that form part of the Peak Wilderness region.

The growing number of visitors makes responsible behaviour particularly important. Pilgrims and tourists are encouraged to avoid littering, respect religious customs and protect the natural surroundings.

The mountain can also experience challenging weather conditions. Rain, strong winds, slippery steps and low visibility may affect the climb. Visitors should follow local advice and avoid taking unnecessary risks.

During the busiest periods, particularly around full moon days and public holidays, the route can become crowded. Allowing extra time for the ascent and descent is therefore a sensible part of planning.

An experience that reveals another side of Sri Lanka

Sri Lanka is often celebrated for its beaches, ancient cities, wildlife and tea-covered hills. Yet Sri Pada offers something different: an opportunity to experience the island through its living traditions and spiritual heritage.

The climb may be demanding, and the night may be long, but the atmosphere of the pilgrimage, the sight of the illuminated path and the first light appearing over the mountains create a truly memorable experience.

As the 2026–2027 season begins on 23 December, another generation of pilgrims will make their way towards the sacred summit.

For those travelling through Sri Lanka during this period, witnessing the pilgrimage or taking part in the climb can offer a deeper understanding of the island and the traditions that continue to shape its identity.

Sri Pada is more than a mountain to climb. It is a journey of faith, endurance and discovery.
